subject: Speed of an animal that is stationary

messages.author: d8c3e4454d06ba83
messages.subject: Speed of an animal that is stationary
parts:
Hi Chris and the rest of the group!

I have started using ctmm to estimate the instantaneous speed of hedgehogs tagged with GPS. I want to analyze their nocturnal activity pattern and potential differences between males and females. The GPS devices (I-gotU) record the individual's position every 3 minutes, only during the nights. I have estimated the error of the devices using the uere.fit function, utilizing 2 of the GPS units at two different locations.

The estimated instantaneous speed decreases to approximately constant values during time intervals that appear to be periods when the hedgehog is stationary. However, this minimum speed is not zero but rather a higher value. As an example, I have attached an image corresponding to an individual tracked over 7 nights. The fitted model (using ctmm.guess and ctmm.select based on the script from Noonan et al. 2019) is "OUF anisotropic error." In this graph, the minimum speed is approximately 65 m/hour.

Graph all nigths attached

Example of a graph for one of the nights (night 5):

 Graph nigth 5 attached

I think that this minimum speed is likely a result of the model not being able to completely eliminate the GPS error when the animal is stationary and possibly hidden in a spot where the signal reception is poor. I would appreciate it if you could confirm whether this is the case. I would also like to ask if it would be correct to adjust the speeds for each night by subtracting the minimum speed for that night so that the speed when the animal is stationary would approximate zero.

For the case of night 5 mentioned earlier, the graph would become the following with that correction:

Graph nigth 5 corrected attached

Thank you very much!


Germán López

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Speed of an animal that is stationary
parts:
Hi Germán,

I would add to those plots the CIs and the mean estimate from speed(FIT), which is the background prediction that the model reverts to in the absence of data. We have some preliminary code to detrend this, but it isn't thoroughly tested yet.

If the hedgehog has inactive periods, then the stationary models can't capture this and will model one mean speed (and variation) for both active and inactive periods. In this case, you could segment first, and then you could fit one stationary model to the active-period data. We will have in-built segmentation methods for this within a couple of years.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Speed of an animal that is stationary
parts:
Thank you very much for your response! 😊

I’m attaching graphs from several nights of the same hedgehog, adding confidence intervals for the instantaneous speed and the average speed obtained with speed(FIT) (green line). Regarding the latter, I'm not sure if I’ve calculated it correctly. The function speed(FIT) gives a value of 2.828777 km/day, so I simply divided that value in meters and its confidence interval by 24 hours (= 117.86 m/h). Would that be correct?

On all nights, the minimum instantaneous speed is below the confidence interval of the average speed (108 – 128 m/h).

This hedgehog was tracked (GPS were recording) for an average of 6.9 hours each day, only during the nighttime, but the model was fitted using all the tracking days together, so the data have gaps between one night and the next.

Generally, hedgehogs have several periods of inactivity each night between periods of activity. I wonder if I were to segment each night into periods of activity and inactivity and fit the model only to the activity periods, would there be enough data in the activity period to fit the model?

Best regards

Germán

PD: sorry the legend is in Spanish: noche = night

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Speed of an animal that is stationary
parts:
Hi Germán,

You can try this code to detrend the mean prediction, but it isn't well tested:

SPD <- speeds(DATA,FIT,level=NA)
# unconditional speeds
MEAN <- FIT
MEAN$error[] <- Inf
MEAN <- speeds(DATA,MEAN,level=NA)
# detrend the unconditional prediction (chi^2)
SPD$est <- sqrt(pmax(SPD$DOF*SPD$est^2-MEAN$DOF*MEAN$est^2,0)/pmax(SPD$DOF-MEAN$DOF,0))
SPD$DOF <- SPD$DOF-MEAN$DOF
CI <- t(sapply(1:nrow(SPD),function(i){sqrt(ctmm:::chisq.ci(SPD$est[i]^2,DOF=SPD$DOF[i]))}))
SPD$low <- CI[,1]
SPD$high <- CI[,3]

The alternative would be segmentation. I suspect the amount of data would be enough, as long as you only remove the bulk of the inactive segments and not the beginning/ends.

Best,
Chris
